candidates.title: Failure Recovery via Belief Updates and World Modeling for Long-Horizon Agents
candidates.abstract: Long-horizon agents often struggle to recover from failures whose causes lie several steps earlier, beyond what local reflection or backtracking can resolve. We introduce BELIEFWEAVER, a framework that combines persistent evidence across attempts with prospective reasoning over repair directions. It maintains a relational belief state over frontiers, attempts, observations, and checkpoints. Execution evidence updates related frontier priorities across attempts and rollback, while diagnostic evidence gates execution. An implicit world model (IWM) evaluates repair hypotheses, predicts progress, and identifies relations among frontiers to guide exploration. We further distill these recurring IWM reasoning components into a 9B student through supervised fine-tuning and on-policy distillation (OPD). Across three terminal-based benchmarks, BELIEFWEAVER improves aggregate final score by 5.1 percentage points over native Terminus-2 continuation, with positive trends in exploration efficiency. The distilled 9B student improves final score by 9.8 percentage points over the reported native baseline while reducing estimated teacher API cost by 54.8% relative to the matched teacher. These results show that persistent evidence and prospective reasoning can improve recovery in long-horizon agent tasks while substantially reducing reliance on teacher-model inference.
candidates.estimate_basis: 20 minute maximum bounded check allocation; not measured runtime

candidates.title: FastVLA: Task-Conditioned and Temporally Adaptive Visual Token Compression for Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models
candidates.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models present a promising paradigm for general-purpose robot manipulation, but closed-loop deployment is often limited by inference efficiency: at each timestep, high-resolution, often multi-view images are encoded into hundreds of visual tokens that dominate transformer computation and latency. Token compression via attention is a natural solution but is challenging for VLA control because (1) decision-critical tokens are determined by the task, not generic visual saliency, and (2) the token budget varies substantially across steps, so static metrics and budgets waste computation or discard control-critical tokens. We introduce FastVLA, a training-free, task-aware, and temporally adaptive visual token compression framework. At each step, FastVLA scores token importance via task-to-vision attention and adaptively sets the compression rate from the importance-distribution uniformity, measured by an inverse-Simpson metric with online sliding-window calibration. We evaluate FastVLA on OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, and CogACT across LIBERO and SIMPLER, and on a physical Franka Research 3 robot. In simulation, it reduces LLM-backbone FLOPs by 35-59\% and action latency by 9-32\% (a 1.09$\times$-1.46$\times$ speedup) while maintaining task success, achieving a comparable or better efficiency-performance trade-off than existing plug-and-play token compression/pruning/reuse baselines. On the real robot, it cuts end-to-end latency by 20\% (1.25$\times$ speedup) at comparable success. Code is available at https://github.com/jiuyixu25/FastVLA.

candidates.title: From Approval to Abuse: Privilege Escalation Attacks on Harness-Protected Coding Agents
candidates.abstract: Coding agents use execution harnesses to constrain the consequences of prompt injection by enforcing permission boundaries. These systems deterministically intercept any out-of-sandbox action and prompt the user for approval. To reduce approval fatigue, users can approve allow-rules proposed by the agent, after which any future action matching the rule is allowed without a prompt. In this work, we show that this mechanism introduces a new risk: untrusted context can influence the permissions presented for approval, with consequences extending beyond the immediate task. We investigate privilege escalation targeting this permission-update process. Specifically, adversarial context planted in a repository can reliably steer an agent performing a routine task into requesting a plausibly justified, yet dangerously broad allow-rule. If the user approves the request, the saved rule can effectively blind the harness, enabling adversaries to execute malicious actions that would otherwise require approval, without triggering human oversight. Across production platforms, including Claude Code and Codex CLI, we demonstrate that agents successfully elicit the target allow-rules in 58% of experimental instances. Once acquired, these rules exhibit a massive semantic blast radius, covering 56.9% of category-specific capability test cases. To further quantify the downstream risk, we show that conditional on rule approval, our exploit achieves verified, silent goal completion in 47 of the 58 eligible instances (81.0%), undermining the safety promise of human-in-the-loop oversight.

candidates.title: From Pixels to Semantics: Edge AI for UAV-Based Critical Infrastructure Inspection
candidates.abstract: Critical infrastructure assets such as bridges, tunnels, dams, and power line networks require timely and scalable inspection. While conventional manual inspection remains costly and hazardous, unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-based inspection has emerged as an efficient alternative for monitoring difficult-to-access structures. Existing UAV inspection pipelines have evolved from cloud-centric offline processing toward edge-based perception using lightweight object detectors such as YOLO for real- time defect localization. This article explores the transition toward fully edge-native semantic inspection powered by lightweight vision language models (VLMs), where UAVs move beyond object detection toward contextual structural understanding. It categorizes existing UAV inspection architectures, identifies their key system challenges and architectural requirements, and experimentally assesses the feasibility of semantic edge intelligence on NVIDIA Jetson UAV-class hardware using the COCO-Bridge dataset. The evaluation integrates a fine-tuned YOLO-26M for object localization and a lightweight SmolVLM-256 for semantic reasoning. Finally, it outlines future directions toward agentic, autonomous, trustworthy, and collaborative semantic UAV inspection across the edge-cloud continuum.

candidates.title: GAIDA: Generative AI for Human-in-the-Loop Document Annotation
candidates.abstract: Document annotation is a fundamental yet labor-intensive step in building document information extraction systems. While Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and Large Language Models (LLMs) can automate parts of this process, we argue that annotation systems should be judged not by how completely they remove human effort, but by how effectively they redirect it toward review and correction. We propose a modular human-in-the-loop architecture that integrates OCR-based extraction, LLM-based semantic pre-annotation, and human validation in a single editable workflow, and present \textbf{GAIDA}, a research prototype serving as its reference implementation. GAIDA supports interchangeable OCR engines, LLM backends, and prompt configurations, and enables stage-specific measurement of annotation effort. In an initial single-annotator, stage-specific study on the FUNSD scanned-form and WildReceipt retail-receipt benchmarks, OCR assistance reduced region-creation and transcription time by up to \textbf{80.9\%}, and reviewing LLM pre-annotations reduced semantic-labeling time by up to \textbf{73.7\%}, despite imperfect pre-annotations of 78.86\% and 86.98\% Micro F1 on FUNSD and WildReceipt, respectively. Finally, we reuse the same implementation, adapting only OCR and prompt configuration, to build and openly release \textbf{AraReceipt}, a manually annotated dataset of 100 Arabic receipt images labeled with 25 key-information classes. The results indicate that imperfect automated outputs provide practical value when presented as editable suggestions under human control.

candidates.title: HexaShell: A Thin Harness for Exploring the Limits of VLM Agents as Robot Coding Agents
candidates.abstract: Agents built on vision language models (VLMs) now compete with learned policies on robot manipulation leaderboards. We ask how far a coding agent can go when it controls a robot instead of a computer, and where it stops. Our system, HexaShell, keeps the harness thin: it only turns the agent's commands into robot motion. The agent drives a robot with two arms through one command line. It sees three RGB cameras and knows their calibration. After each failed attempt, the agent reads the log, finds the cause, and writes or fixes small programs called tools. In this way it keeps what it learns as code, as a coding agent does when it fixes a failing test. The tools may use only what the robot observes. They use triangulation to find where objects are, relative to each other and to the gripper. If two cameras see the same point, the point lies where the two camera rays meet. If a point lies on a known plane, such as the table or the top of a block, it lies where its ray meets that plane. When the head camera is not enough, the robot moves a wrist camera to get a second view. We build the tools on only ten layouts of one seed per task, then freeze them and test them on ten new layouts of the same seed. We use Codex with GPT-6-Astra at medium reasoning effort. On all 42 RoboDojo tasks, HexaShell reaches a success rate of 39.7% and a progress score of 48.0, averaged in the same way as the leaderboard. This is a new state of the art on RoboDojo. The limit is contact, not reasoning: pushing reaches 92.5% and memory tasks 65.0%, but tight insertion only 8.3%. When the agent fails, it usually sees the failure but cannot make the motion work. We open source the tools evolved so far at https://github.com/HexaFuture/HexaShell.

candidates.title: How Far Can Coding Agents Go in Visual Generation?
candidates.abstract: Modern image generation largely relies on specialized generative models that leave the process of image construction implicit in learned parameters. We explore an alternative: general-purpose coding agents that construct images through executable programs. Our study of zero-shot drawing on AgentDrawBench, a 200-prompt benchmark, reveals a distinctive capability profile. Agents excel at preserving structure and satisfying precise visual constraints, achieving competitive results in domains where compositional accuracy matters more than photorealistic appearance, while remaining limited in perceptual richness. Their visual expressiveness varies with the drawing interface, and a qualitative study on reconstruction shows how procedural skills extracted from human demonstrations support different artistic media. We then examine code as an external visual language of thought: a structured, executable representation that agents can construct and inspect. We test it in visual question answering task and find reconstructed visual code retains substantial information for question answering and, in some domains, supports higher accuracy than the original image. These abilities raise a further question: do agents draw on a shared internal representation of scene content beyond a particular drawing program? We explore an internal visual language-of-thought hypothesis, in which a shared, compositionally structured representation supports visual operations across drawing languages. Cross-harness drawings and images assembled from independent single-pixel queries exhibit related layouts and tones. Agents also maintain self-generated room arrangements across viewpoints after visible drawings are removed. These results demonstrate that the coding agent would maintain a consistent and coherent world inside its imagine even before the harness gets involved and the generation starts.

candidates.title: HPCAgent-Bench: A Framework for Sound Benchmarking of Code-Optimizing Agents, Harnesses, and Skills
candidates.abstract: Coding agents are increasingly used to optimize code, but existing benchmarks fix one accelerator, programming model or harness, so they cannot isolate what each component contributes or show whether added skills and tools repay their cost. We present HPCAgent-Bench with 689 kernels in three tracks: loop-level optimization challenges, kernels extracted from HPC codes, and machine-learning models. The framework specifies each kernel once in NumPy, derives C and Fortran references, accepts submissions through a common C ABI or Python interface, and runs them on CPUs or GPUs, on one or multiple nodes. An external judge checks correctness on hidden fuzzed inputs and times each submission, closing paths agents use to exploit the testing system. We introduce two metrics for reporting results: \textit{intervention efficacy} measures an intervention, such as adding a tool, through paired runs on speedup, success rate and cost, and \textit{weighted token cost} reports input, cached-input and output tokens under explicit weights. Agents reach up to $4.2\times$ speedup over automatic parallelizers, and their optimizations transfer to another machine: $93$--$99\%$ of answers without device-specific code remain correct, and per-kernel speedups keep a rank correlation of $r_s\ge0.84$. Across 40 matched setups, interventions significantly change speedup only twice but token cost by up to $3.0\times$. Because token weighting decides whether a saving is significant, we state the weights and release every token count as a standard for cost reporting. We provide the first comprehensive, broad and hardened benchmark for the sound evaluation of agentic optimization, with transparent cost metrics.

candidates.title: Improving Environment-Agnostic Coding Agents: The Role of Scaffolding
candidates.abstract: Stronger language models may increasingly construct useful procedures for themselves, reducing the advantage of developer-supplied scaffolding. We investigate why this advantage persists and whether an environment-agnostic agent can be improved without environment-specific engineering. We evaluate a Codex-based agent in two nearly identical prompt variants on ARC-AGI-3, AGI Maze, and Terminal-Bench. Each variant is deployed with unchanged code, prompts, and general-purpose tools across environments, receiving environment-specific information as input. Changing only an instruction to encourage reporting difficulties and returning control for automatic continuation improves mean scores on both ARC-AGI-3 and AGI Maze, while Terminal-Bench shows small, mixed changes. Yet the general agent remains below an ARC-AGI-3-specific reference, including with GPT-5.6-sol. The reference prescribes organization and control rather than supplying new game rules or solutions. To investigate this gap, we transfer reset decisions to a scripted controller that follows a convention already given to the agent. This small change recovers part of the specialized agent's advantage. A complementary AGI Maze experiment shows that additional tutorial experience can reduce performance. Together, these findings highlight the distinction between having information and tools available and using them effectively. Supplied procedures still matter for the models tested here. The performance gains also come with higher token-based cost. The experiments do not separate better use of information and procedures from additional or differently allocated inference. We provide the EnvTraverse framework and an evaluated baseline agent for testing whether further environment-independent changes improve performance in some environments without degrading it in others.

candidates.title: Interaction-as-a-Judge
candidates.abstract: Coding agents are tasked with producing sophisticated interactive applications such as websites, desktop applications, and games. While humans assess these applications interactively, current automated LLM evaluations primarily focus on code analysis and unit tests. This mismatch can cause LLM judges to miss failures that are immediately apparent to human users. We study Interaction-as-a-Judge, an evaluation paradigm where computer-use agents (CUAs) directly interact with an application. We demonstrate that Interaction-as-a-Judge can improve both evaluation and generation of interactive applications. To this end, we collect and release two complementary datasets: $6,858$ pairs of applications with human preferences and corresponding agent traces, and $222$ applications with human-verified requirement labels. Relative to standard non-interactive approaches, we find that Interaction-as-a-Judge improves evaluation in terms of predicting human preferences ($65.6\% \to 69.1\%$) and requirement verification ($77.0\% \to 81.6\%$). We also observe scaling benefits: across both preference alignment and requirement verification, higher-quality interactions improve performance. Finally, through both inference- and training-time experiments, we demonstrate that Interaction-as-a-Judge can also improve the quality of generated artifacts. At inference time, Interaction-as-a-Judge repairs $75.5\%$ of broken requirements within five attempts, compared to $55.4\%$ for code-only self-feedback. At training time, using Interaction-as-a-Judge as a reward signal improves win-rate over the base model by $6.7$pp while reducing both generated code length by $35.7\%$ and build failure rates by $7.2$pp compared to a code-only reward signal.

candidates.title: Lightweight Machine Learning for Classifying Disaster-Related Social Media Posts
candidates.abstract: Classifying disaster-related social-media posts into humanitarian information labels is challenging because individual messages are typically short and context-limited, humanitarian categories can overlap semantically, and the CrisisBench label distribution is strongly imbalanced. This study investigates whether lightweight lexical machine-learning methods can provide effective and computationally efficient classification under these conditions. Using the CrisisBench v1.0 English humanitarian task, comprising 87,455 records across predefined Train, Development and Test splits, we conduct a controlled comparison of TF-IDF representations and lightweight classifiers, with Macro-F1 as the primary model-selection metric. Beyond aggregate predictive performance, the study jointly examines per-label behaviour, directional error patterns, relative decision margins, computational requirements, and the effect of domain-specific training through a tropical-cyclone specialist model. The selected balanced LinearSVC with unigram-bigram TF-IDF and C=0.5 achieved an Accuracy of 0.8282, a Macro-F1 of 0.6578 and a Weighted-F1 of 0.8315 on the held-out Test split. Lower decision margins were substantially associated with prediction errors, while the tropical-cyclone specialist achieved modestly higher in-domain aggregate performance with substantially lower feature and fitting requirements. The study contributes a controlled, label-sensitive and resource-aware evaluation of lightweight humanitarian text classification that characterises not only aggregate performance, but also where these models fail and how their behaviour changes under domain-specific training.

candidates.title: Lightweight Vision Models for Galaxy Morphology Classification: A Comparative Study of ResNet, MobileNet, EfficientNet, and MobileViT on Galaxy10 DECaLS
candidates.abstract: <jats:p>Automated galaxy morphology classification now rests on parameter-heavy convolutional backbones, whose cost becomes a design constraint as survey volumes grow. This paper compares three lightweight architectures (MobileNetV2, EfficientNetB0, and MobileViT-Extra Small (XS)) against a ResNet50 baseline on the Galaxy10 Dark Energy Camera Legacy Survey (DECaLS) benchmark of 17,736 images in ten classes, holding data splits, augmentation, optimizer, loss, and stopping rule fixed so that the backbone is the only variable. The lightweight models give up between 2.07 and 2.55 percentage points of support-weighted accuracy while removing 82.9% to 91.8% of the parameters and 42% to 59% of the per-image inference latency, which makes them 5.7 to 11.8 times more efficient per parameter. Two results run against expectations. The hardest class is not the rarest one. In a redshift-stratified comparison, the only attention-based backbone falls furthest behind the baseline on exactly the smallest and faintest galaxies, so the advantage reported for Vision Transformers does not carry over to a lightweight hybrid. For survey-scale processing, the trade is worth making; for a catalogue of a few thousand galaxies, it is not.</jats:p>

candidates.title: Mallea: Building, Steering, and Memorizing Worlds with Coding Agent
candidates.abstract: Code world models represent world dynamics through explicit state and executable rules. We investigate how to coordinate object representations, behavioral revisions, and visual memory within this formulation. We present Mallea, a system for building, steering, and memorizing worlds from text. A coding agent infers object interaction requirements from the prompt and jointly plans object structure, properties, and rules, favoring compact representations that support those requirements. The world evolves under the planned rules; optional user actions steer it, while text requests can edit properties or extend capabilities with unaffected state preserved. Object texture memory retains reusable appearance only for whitebox-defined objects and adapts it as those objects change. The program advances world state, while a generative renderer combines current structure with remembered appearance. By organizing construction, intervention, and memory around the same objects, Mallea conditions subsequent observations on the latest state and compatible appearance. Project page: https://lxycopper.github.io/Mallea.

candidates.title: MMSearch-OPD: Easy Made Hard, Hard Made Learnable for Long-Horizon Multimodal Search Agents
candidates.abstract:
Multimodal deep search is moving from short queries to long-horizon investigations that continually acquire evidence. However, training such agents remains constrained by limited challenging training questions and insufficient process feedback.
  We introduce MMSearch-OPD, combining controllable data refinement with joint reinforcement learning (RL) and on-policy distillation (OPD). Our Refine pipeline performs targeted expansion of reasoning chains derived from existing simple multimodal questions. Parameterized transformations control search depth and cross-modal evidence requirements while reusing existing image--question pairs. For training, answer rewards and lightweight behavior penalties guide RL, while the reward gap modulates token-level teacher guidance on imperfect student trajectories. An exponentially decaying distillation coefficient reduces teacher dependence as training proceeds.
  Experiments show gains from data refinement and further improvements from joint training after SFT, indicating stronger long-horizon multimodal deep search capabilities.
candidates.estimate_basis: 20 minute maximum bounded check allocation; not measured runtime

candidates.title: OfficeTown: Generative Organizations for Evolving Agent Intelligence
candidates.abstract: AI agents increasingly use files and software tools to produce professional deliverables. Such work draws on materials, decisions, and feedback accumulated across assignments. We introduce OfficeTown, a generative simulation framework for professional organizations in which tasks and their context arise from continuing organizational work. From a natural-language description of an organization's purpose and activities, OfficeTown initializes an organization whose members coordinate work, delegate bounded assignments to assistant agents, and review their deliverables. Artifacts, decisions, and unresolved matters persist and shape subsequent work, while responsibilities and permissions determine what each member can see and do. We curate work requests, their context, and review feedback into executable resources for evaluation and learning. We construct OfficeTown Bench with 406 tasks and 4,836 evaluation criteria from 23 simulated organizations across eight professional domains, incorporating domain-expert feedback. Frontier-model evaluations reveal substantial remaining headroom. Supervised fine-tuning and on-policy distillation on OfficeTown data substantially improve Qwen3.5-9B on external professional-work benchmarks, including GDPval. Supplementary evaluations show that the principal--assistant harness achieves higher scores than the single- and multi-agent baselines tested. These results highlight the value of organizational simulation in generating work-grounded data and environments for the continued development of generalist agents.

candidates.title: ReproBAIT: Can coding agents build their own biological AI tools?
candidates.abstract: Large language models are increasingly competent at leveraging scientific knowledge and existing computational tools to execute complex workflows. At present, little information exists on their ability to reconstruct tools when given limited descriptions of such tools. We introduce an evaluation titled ReproBAIT (Reproducing Biological AI Tools), which measures the ability of coding agents to design, implement, and train biological AI tools taken from published research across a range of information access conditions. The coding agent is securely sandboxed without internet access and receives training data, a fixed time and compute budget, and limited information about the tool to replicate. We then score the reproduced biological AI tool based on its performance (tool-specific metrics) on held-out data. We evaluated a set of biological AI tools of varying complexities: ProteinMPNN, an inverse protein folding tool, RFdiffusion3, an all-atom generative diffusion tool, and a closed-source molecular design tool. We institute a methodology to check for memorisation, as the open source tools are likely to be included in models' pretraining corpus. Across a range of leading closed- and open-source coding agents, we find substantial reproduction capability for some selected tools, though limited capability for a highly complex tool. We find moderate evidence consistent with memorisation, varying across coding agents. These results suggest that tool developers need to be increasingly cautious when releasing information about the tools publicly; re-creation of the tool based on such information could undermine a tool's commercial value or invalidate dual-use managed access strategies.

candidates.title: RoboSimStudio: An Interactive Toolkit for Human and Agent Rapid Real2Sim of Robot Manipulation Tasks
candidates.abstract: It has been difficult to accurately model the physics of the interaction between a robot and the objects it manipulates, including contact mechanics, coupled contact dynamics, deformations, stiffness and friction. We present RoboSimStudio (RSS), an interactive toolkit that makes choices of solver, contact model, and physical parameters explicit and editable, allowing both humans and coding agents to quickly create and iteratively refine simulations based on observed physical behavior. We implement RSS with the open Newton physics simulation system and describe experiments with human-guided real2sim using (1) visual evaluation, (2) force-feedback and (3) agentic Real2Sim2Real. Code, video and additional information can be found on the project website: https://robosimstudio.github.io

candidates.title: Rubrics from the Task, Verdicts from Evidence: Pointwise Rubric Rewards with Tool-Augmented Judges
candidates.abstract: Rubric-based reward models (RMs) evaluate responses against explicit criteria. However, existing methods often derive criteria from observed response candidates, introducing response-induced bias that may limit rubric generalizability. Their judges also struggle with mechanical constraints when relying on reading alone, and commonly used pairwise judges provide only relative preferences, complicating their direct use for policy optimization. We propose ReVeR, a pointwise rubric RM that derives hard rules and graded principles by reasoning about the instruction alone and evaluates responses independently through tool-augmented judging. Both components are trained through label-blind distillation, in which preference labels only filter a teacher's outputs, yielding ReVeR-Traces, a large-scale dataset of rubric-reasoning and judging trajectories. Experiments demonstrate that ReVeR outperforms pairwise rubric RMs in average preference accuracy, most clearly on instruction following, as well as in test-time scaling and downstream policy optimization. We further find that generator RL improves preference accuracy while reducing rubric fidelity, and that higher preference accuracy does not necessarily translate into better downstream policies. These findings highlight that rubric fidelity, preference accuracy, and downstream utility are distinct properties, shedding light on future RM research.

candidates.title: Scaling Online Exploration for Robot Agents
candidates.abstract: Robot learning has advanced by scaling demonstration datasets and model capacity; however, deploying a new robot embodiment or task typically necessitates a dedicated teleoperation corpus. The resulting policies remain bounded by their imitation distributions, limiting generalization and continual self-improvement. We introduce RAX (Robot Agent eXploration), an open-source framework for robot agents centered on scaling exploration: enabling agents to improve by acquiring online experience and synthesizing executable programs. In RAX, a general-purpose coding agent generates robot control code, operating without action demonstration data, hand-engineered action primitives, or value-function guidance. Through online exploration, the agent identifies decision sequences that achieve task goals and compiles them into modular programs encapsulating the full perception-planning-control loop. Using RAX, we present a systematic multi-embodiment study on scaling online exploration across precision and long-horizon manipulation tasks using single-arm, bimanual, dexterous, mobile, and humanoid systems in simulation and on real robots. Generalization performance on unseen environments improves consistently as exploration scales. In simulation, RAX outperforms top baseline models by +37.4% on average. On real robots, RAX autonomously learns memory-dependent, articulated, high-precision, deformable, and long-horizon mobile manipulation tasks without human demonstrations, continually improving performance by composing verified skills from prior exploration sessions. As exploration scales, we observe emergent capabilities including active perception, error recovery, safety guardrails, and human-robot collaboration. We open-source RAX as a generalist robot-agent platform in which new robot embodiments are integrated through their APIs alone, without teleoperated data collection or policy training.

candidates.title: SERO: Learning from Executable Oracle Continuations for Long-Horizon Agentic Reinforcement Learning
candidates.abstract: Long-horizon agentic RL is constrained by the futures visited by the current policy. When rollouts fail to reach useful behaviors, improved credit assignment cannot provide supervision for states and actions that were never encountered. On-policy distillation (OPD) introduces teacher guidance on policy-induced states, and recent multi-turn variants improve how this guidance is scheduled, replayed, refined, or validated. However, they do not directly use the oracle-controlled future itself as the training trajectory. We introduce State-Rooted Executable Rollout Optimization (SERO), which augments on-policy agentic RL with executable oracle continuations. SERO restores a state actually reached by the current policy and lets a training-only oracle continue interacting with the real environment, making the downstream observations and oracle actions themselves available for learning. It then applies policy-reachability weighting, which weights each oracle step by the frozen behavior policy's compatibility with the preceding oracle actions. This allows deeper supervision to become effective as the policy becomes more compatible with the oracle branch. The oracle loss is optimized separately from the base RL estimator and no oracle is used at inference time. We evaluate SERO on two challenging interactive-agent benchmarks, ALFWorld and WebShop, using Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. On ALFWorld, learning the full executable continuation is substantially more effective than supervising only the root oracle action, while policy-reachability weighting further improves out-of-distribution performance.

candidates.title: Spatial Memory by Agents, for Agents
candidates.abstract: Spatial memory enables robots to reuse past observations for localization, navigation, and question answering. Designing such memory involves jointly deciding what to retain and how to retrieve it for diverse semantic, metric, and temporal needs. We investigate whether coding agents can automate this design process through iterative implementation and evaluation. Under a fixed development budget, a Designer Agent writes and revises code for memory construction and retrieval using feedback from a fixed Query Agent. The resulting implementations are frozen before building memories from held-out observation histories, without access to downstream questions, and evaluated across five complementary task tracks using the same Query Agent. Across three independent design searches, Codex / GPT-6 Astra averages 44.23 on the equally weighted five-track score, versus 29.32 for ReMEmbR, the strongest evaluated baseline supporting all five tracks, a 50.9% relative improvement. Qualitative analysis relates performance differences to evidence retention and retrieval, while identifying grounding and evidence-use failures. These results demonstrate the potential of coding agents to automate spatial memory design, while revealing task-dependent trade-offs in performance and computational cost. Project page: https://ba-fa-3344.github.io/.

candidates.title: Spectral World Renderer: Unified 3D Hyperspectral Unmixing
candidates.abstract: Cameras and the foundation models built on them recognize what a 3D scene contains, but not what it is made of: surfaces of the same colour can be different materials. Hyperspectral unmixing explains each spectrum as a mixture of material signatures, yet in 3D it is applied to rendered images after the views are composited, or tied to slow implicit fields, and no multi-view data with known composition exist to check the result. We present the Spectral World Renderer (SWR), which unifies world generation and unmixing. A coding agent builds executable 3D worlds that are rendered with measured spectra, so every hyperspectral image comes with exact labels and sub-pixel proportions; the resulting SWR-Bench provides eight indoor and outdoor worlds in which decompositions can be verified. SWR then unmixes inside rendering: each Gaussian of a compact 3D representation is decoded into material abundances before compositing, so one render yields spectra and material maps, and any surface can be queried by material name, a clicked pixel or a reference spectrum. Without material labels, SWR identifies materials best in all eight worlds, has the best mean PSNR on real captures, trains 3.7-12.9x faster than unmixing baselines, renders 34.9 labelled views/s and separates same-coloured materials.

candidates.title: State-Aware Generation of Deployable Websites from Visual Prototypes and Requirements
candidates.abstract: Generating deployable websites from visual prototypes and textual requirements is increasingly feasible with multimodal models, yet keeping generated projects consistent with their prototypes remains challenging. Prototypes specify layouts and visual elements, while requirements describe interaction workflows and deployment constraints. Existing UI-to-code methods and coding agents often treat layout reconstruction, interaction implementation, and project editing separately, allowing visual elements, files, workflows, dependencies, and render evidence to lose their correspondence across generation, verification, and update. We call this problem prototype-to-project state drift. We propose VisStateCoder, a state-aware framework that maintains these correspondences in a Project State Graph. The graph connects four types of state nodes through typed links and supports prototype grounding, graph-guided generation, and render-evidence-guided scoped updates that map failed checks to affected files while preserving files outside the update scope. We evaluate VisStateCoder on Vision2Web using five foundation models across Static Webpage, Interactive Frontend, and Full-Stack Website tasks. Averaged across models, VisStateCoder improves overall scores over the strongest baseline for each model by 26.1 and 22.6 points on Interactive Frontend and Full-Stack Website tasks, respectively. It also reduces verified-state drift, measured by checks that pass in one update round but fail later, compared with alternative state representations. An annotation study of 50 tasks finds that the constructed graphs achieve 95.6% edge-level F1.

candidates.title: SWE-at-Scale: Scalable Issue Synthesis from Historical Bug Fixes
candidates.abstract: As coding agents become increasingly capable, robust evaluation requires a broader and more diverse supply of verifiable software engineering (SWE) tasks. However, real-world tasks are constrained by the natural frequency of issue reporting and the substantial cost of manual curation. Furthermore, existing synthetic approaches rely primarily on the pretrained knowledge of large models coupled with heuristic prompting, often failing to capture the authentic, complex mechanics of software failures. To exponentially scale SWE task production, we introduce SWE-at-Scale, a framework that automatically synthesizes realistic issues by reverse-engineering real-world software fixes. Our key insight is that historical fixes encapsulate deep mechanistic knowledge of bug formation: inverting a fix transforms repair supervision into bug-induction supervision grounded in actual development scenarios. SWE-at-Scale transfers these learned bug patterns to novel code contexts, repeatedly sampling diverse bug typologies to construct executable SWE tasks. Extensive experiments show that SWE-at-Scale generates more diverse and realistic SWE tasks than current synthesis baselines while posing greater challenges to state-of-the-art coding agents. Notably, SWE-at-Scale can generate distinct bug types from a single code context, with bug diversity scaling robustly even up to 200 generations per file. Overall, SWE-at-Scale turns finite real-world fixes into reusable supervision for scalable synthesis of realistic, diverse, and challenging SWE tasks.

candidates.title: SWE-MISBEHAVIOR: Benchmarking and Mitigating Boundary Violations in Software Coding Agents
candidates.abstract: We present SWE-MISBEHAVIOR, the first taxonomy and evaluation framework for diagnosing boundary-violating misbehaviors in coding agents. It contains 7.4K human-in-the-loop synthesized samples spanning three layers of agent action space: (i) Code Generation, (ii) File Management, and (iii) System Interaction. Across these categories, SWE-MISBEHAVIOR covers 11 distinct misbehaviors with a fully automated evaluation protocol, including coding-action violations, Create/Read/Update/Delete (CRUD) file misbehaviors, system integrity and abuse violations, and task-goal misalignment. Experiments on state-of-the-art open-source coding agents (e.g., OpenHands, smolagents) reveal substantial misaligned behaviors, including dependency misinterpretation (up to 98.5% of cases), unintended modification of user inputs (50.5%), and silent compromise of environment integrity (53%). Motivated by these findings, we further propose CODE-KIT, a lightweight adaptive framework that combines misbehavior-aware guidelines with novel tools to help agents avoid such failures. CODE-KIT reduces misbehaviors by 52% for smolagents and 34% for OpenHands, while simultaneously improving task completion performance.

candidates.title: TCP-SSM: Efficient Vision State Space Models with Token-Conditioned Poles
candidates.abstract: State Space Models (SSMs) have emerged as a compelling alternative to attention models for long-range vision tasks, offering input-dependent recurrence with linear complexity. However, most efficient SSM variants reduce computation cost by modifying scan routes, resolutions, or traversal patterns, while largely leaving the recurrent dynamics implicit. Consequently, the model's state-dependent memory behavior is difficult to control, particularly in compact backbones where long scan paths can exceed the effective memory horizon. We propose Token-Conditioned Poles SSM (TCP-SSM), a structured selective SSM framework that improves efficiency while making recurrence dynamics explicit and interpretable through stable poles. TCP-SSM builds each scan operator with 1) real poles that model monotone or sign-alternating decay, and 2) complex-conjugate poles that capture damped oscillatory responses. Using bounded radius and angle modulation, TCP-SSM converts shared base poles into token-dependent poles, allowing each scan step to adapt its memory behavior to the current visual token while preserving pole stability. For practical scalability, we integrate grouped pole sharing with a lightweight low-rank input pathway, yielding an efficient scan operator that preserves linear-time scan complexity. Across image classification, semantic segmentation, and object detection, TCP-SSM reduces SSM computation complexity up to 44% in Vision Mamba-style models while maintaining or surpassing baseline accuracy.

candidates.title: Temporal Reasoning Pipeline: Enhancing Lightweight Vision-Language Models for On-device Anomaly Detection
The Code of Theseus: Can Agents Rebuild Software from Recovered Design Documents?
candidates.abstract: LLM agents increasingly design a system before implementing it, yet the data to train and evaluate them centres on implementation and testing: requirements and design artefacts are often missing, outdated or private. Source code, in contrast, is abundant. Prior work recovers architecture documentation by feeding LLMs the source code or letting agents explore it, which saturates the context, does not scale to many repositories, and yields a single artefact rather than aligned ones. We present a framework that recovers aligned stakeholder intent, requirements and architecture from a compact repository representation, a static dependency graph and key contextual files, and release the artefacts of 10,764 Java, Python, C/C++ and C# repositories as a dataset. An LLM judge rates the artefacts of three generators as clear and internally consistent, but less reliably correct and at the right level of abstraction. To test whether the artefacts carry the design, we pose a software Ship of Theseus: a coding agent rebuilds 29 Commit0 libraries from the intent alone or with the recovered requirements and architecture, given only an interface contract and part of the tests. The artefacts do not significantly change the held-out pass rate (33.7% vs. 35.8%), but bring the rebuilt module structure significantly closer to the original (module F1 from 0.54 to 0.63), with either generator and even with concise artefacts. Recovered artefacts thus convey design that tests do not capture, offering a scalable source of design-level data for agents that design before they implement, and the round trip measures this without human references.

candidates.title: The Last Mile of Coding Agents for Long-Document Tasks: An Empirical Study on Clinical Trial Protocol Digitization
candidates.abstract: Clinical trial protocols serve as the source of truth for study design, but are mostly written and used as unstructured PDF documents. Digitizing protocols turns static content into structured, machine-readable data that clinical software can analyze, validate, and execute. Coding agents, which select tools, execute code, and revise their approach as they work, are increasingly applied to such long-document tasks, yet it remains unclear how reliably they turn complete documents into accurate structured outputs. We study this question using protocol digitization as a testbed. We introduce TrialPD-Bench, an expert-annotated benchmark of 150 publicly available protocol PDFs spanning four task categories. Beyond final-answer performance, our evaluation measures evidence recall from agent traces, agent behavior, and cost. Across nine proprietary and open-weight models in five coding-agent harnesses, even the strongest agents do not fully solve protocol digitization. Our analysis further shows that agents usually locate the required evidence but fail in the last mile of transcribing and structuring it. We further develop TrialScribe, a domain-specific harness that equips coding agents with task skills and a verification loop. TrialScribe improves a locally served open-weight model by 6.2-59.4 points across eight metrics, enabling it to match or surpass proprietary models such as GPT-5.6-Sol.

candidates.title: The Last Remote Sensing Model Built by Humans? Casting Any Earth Observation Task as Recursive Self-Improvement
candidates.abstract: Earth observation (EO) models are still built by hand. For each new task, experts design a training recipe and tune it against a benchmark. We show that this loop can be handed to an agent. Any verifiable task can be cast as a harness and a verifier, where the harness defines what the agent may use and the verifier defines what counts as success. Every EO task can be made verifiable, through labeled benchmarks, independent sensors, physical models or the repeated observation of the same place. Given only these two components, a general-purpose coding agent builds the EO model and improves it recursively on its own outputs. Settings long treated as separate research problems, from learning with a handful of labels to adapting across domains, become choices of harness and verifier. On six EO benchmarks spanning optical, SAR and multispectral time-series imagery, with outputs that range from land-cover maps and ship instances to canopy heights and answers about large images, agent-built models surpass the state of the art on every one, and on land-cover mapping, they do so from 11% of the training labels. This establishes a new paradigm for EO, in which people design harnesses and verifiers and agents build the models, so EO models improve as agents do.

candidates.title: Thinking in Graphs: Neo4j-Backed Exploit-Chain Reasoning for LLM Penetration-Testing Agents
candidates.abstract: LLM coding agents such as Claude Code and OpenAI Codex can drive penetration-testing tools, but they reason about an engagement as a flat list of findings in a context window. Attackers think in graphs: isolated low-severity exposures turn catastrophic once chained through credential capture, privilege escalation, and lateral movement. This gap feeds a common belief that AI agents cannot truly chain exploitation; we argue this describes the flat context window, not the model. We present ChainGraph, a pattern that externalizes exploit-chain reasoning into a Neo4j property graph wired to an off-the-shelf agent via the Model Context Protocol, no bespoke harness. Findings, attack steps, credentials, assets, and tamper-evident evidence receipts are typed nodes with pre/post-condition edges; JSON/Markdown holds documentary memory while Neo4j holds reasoning memory. We formalize five operator questions (next-step inference, entry-to-crown-jewel pathing, combined-severity promotion, evidence provenance, and chokepoint identification) as reusable Cypher and Graph Data Science queries, plus a chain-severity score distinct from per-finding local severity. On a synthetic multi-forest Active Directory engagement modeled on GOAD, in live Neo4j with GDS, three findings rated Medium in isolation become Critical once their path to the forest root is materialized, and betweenness centrality names the best chain break-points. Scoping each decision to a graph result rather than re-reading the engagement cut the reasoning payload by about 98% on a token proxy. We give a reproducible setup for Claude Code and Codex. Results are illustrative single-run measurements, not a benchmark.

candidates.title: TimeRSI: Towards Self-Improved Agentic Deployment for Time-Series Foundation Models
candidates.abstract: Time-series foundation models provide strong zero-shot forecast, but deployment for real-world applications still requires task-specific designs for model inputs and outputs. Direct inference can leave domain knowledge and recurring forecast errors unaddressed, while tailored pipelines require substantial human expertise and effort. We introduce TimeRSI, a self-improving agentic deployment system around frozen forecasting models. A coding agent translates task descriptions into executable pipeline changes. It tests each revision on historical forecasting windows and uses observed errors to guide subsequent revisions. During deployment, an adaptive selector chooses among the resulting pipelines using completed forecasts under similar conditions. Across 198 tasks on TIME and fev-bench, TimeRSI outperforms all submissions on six point and probabilistic forecasting metrics. Controlled comparisons support the value of feedback-guided revision over non-iterative pipeline search. Further experiments verify the generalization with different coding agents and forecasting models. Code is available at https://github.com/haoxin1998/TimeRSI.

candidates.title: TokenEconomizer: Experience-Driven Black-Box Cost Control for Coding Agents
candidates.abstract: Advances in frontier coding agents have sharply increased the token costs of AI-assisted software engineering. Their token efficiency is typically evaluated on isolated tasks, whereas real-world developers use them to continuously build, update, and maintain large-scale projects. This mismatch motivates us to evaluate agents over sequences of realistic coding tasks, where we find that agents exhibit recurring environment-dependent token costs that existing methods struggle to reduce. To minimize these costs, we introduce TokenEconomizer, an external controller that cuts environment-specific token costs over a sequence of tasks. These cuts come from determining (i) which operational micro-skills to inject, (ii) which persistently irrelevant tools to prune, and (iii) when to intervene in unproductive failure loops. Across Claude Code, Codex, and GitHub Copilot CLI paired with frontier models, TokenEconomizer reduces the average token cost by 18.4-30.9% with comparable task success. Savings hold in every repository under every tested agent-model setting and generalize to diverse domains such as sequential web development and security auditing, where costs fall by 6.4-21.2% depending on task structure. Our work establishes adaptive black-box cost control as a promising direction for reducing token costs of coding agents in realistic settings.

candidates.title: ToolRosetta: Surface-Form Invariance of Tool-Call Guards
candidates.abstract: Step-level guards for tool-using agents are evaluated on tidy JSON tool calls, but deployed coding agents act through execute_bash and execute_code tools whose payloads are strings. We introduce ToolRosetta, which re-renders every candidate action in the AgentDojo and AgentHarm splits of TS-Bench as a Python call, as a shell command, and without the agent's rationale. The renderings are produced by code and verified by round-trip parsing, so the user request, the history, the label and the action's effect stay fixed while only the surface form changes. Across eleven guards with two placebo controls, frontier and strong open-weight guards are stable: no frontier error rate moves by more than 3.4 points. Four of five specialized agent guards are not: under the shell form their false-positive rates rise by 21 to 47 points on AgentDojo, and TS-Guard's by 38 points on its own home benchmark, blocking between a third and nine in ten benign actions; the fifth, StepGuard, does not move. A small open guard drifts five points more permissive. Removing the agent's rationale moves most guards whose input carries it, in guard-specific directions. A request-blind control on one guard shows that the rationale is where intent is read from. A parser that restores the canonical call in front of the guard removes the effect for these renderings, by construction. Benchmark accuracy on JSON calls does not predict a guard's operating point behind a code-acting agent.

candidates.title: Towards Agentic Proof Harness Engineering
candidates.abstract: Formal verification of real-world projects requires substantial manual effort, from specifying correctness properties to constructing the infrastructure needed to check them. We envision verification agents that assist developers throughout this process. Among the many tasks involved, one stands out as both foundational and amenable to automation: proof-harness engineering. A proof harness defines an isolated verification environment for a program unit, such as a function or module, by providing symbolic inputs, initialization code, and models of its dependencies. Today, proof-harness engineering remains largely a manual task performed by verification engineers. To explore the potential of coding agents for this task, we propose an agentic proof-harness engineer that automatically constructs verifier-ready harnesses from a software project and a designated verification target. We combine the agent with formal soundness and precision guards to validate generated abstractions and guide their refinement. We evaluate the feasibility of our approach in an exploratory case study on curl and libuv, using three historical assertion violations already embedded in the source code as verification properties. Our results show that the agent successfully constructs proof harnesses that enable CBMC to detect all three violations. We further demonstrate the potential for reusing these harnesses with other verification tools.

candidates.title: TradingAgents: Multi-Agents LLM Financial Trading Framework
candidates.abstract:
Significant progress has been made in automated problem-solving using
societies of agents powered by large language models (LLMs). In finance,
efforts have largely focused on single-agent systems handling specific tasks or
multi-agent frameworks independently gathering data. However, the multi-agent
systems' potential to replicate real-world trading firms' collaborative
dynamics remains underexplored. TradingAgents proposes a novel stock trading
framework inspired by trading firms, featuring LLM-powered agents in
specialized roles such as fundamental analysts, sentiment analysts, technical
analysts, and traders with varied risk profiles. The framework includes Bull
and Bear researcher agents assessing market conditions, a risk management team
monitoring exposure, and traders synthesizing insights from debates and
historical data to make informed decisions. By simulating a dynamic,
collaborative trading environment, this framework aims to improve trading
performance. Detailed architecture and extensive experiments reveal its
superiority over baseline models, with notable improvements in cumulative
returns, Sharpe ratio, and maximum drawdown, highlighting the potential of
multi-agent LLM frameworks in financial trading. TradingAgents is available at
https://github.com/TauricResearch/TradingAgents.
candidates.estimate_basis: 20 minute maximum bounded check allocation; not measured runtime

candidates.title: Training Reasoning Models to Generate Diverse Scientific Ideas
candidates.abstract: One of the first steps of a research pipeline is generating ideas. Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to automate this step, but most of this work optimizes the quality of individual ideas, while overlooking diversity. In our work, we study document-grounded ideation, focusing on increasing the diversity of LLM generated ideas and ensuring they are high quality. Given prior papers, a model must propose a set of ideas that are each high-quality and clearly distinct from one another, while also being grounded in the input documents. To optimize for this, we propose training with a set-level reinforcement learning objective. In our setup, in a single generation, the model writes K structured idea cards grounded in the source papers, and the set is scored jointly, where each idea's quality is weighted by its distance from the ideas written before it. This teaches the model to steer each new idea away from its predecessors. We show that our trained 8B model achieves higher creative utility (a measure combining quality and diversity) than Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-6 Astra on our contamination-free benchmark. In a pilot human study with four experts, our sets are judged as promising as Claude Opus 4.8's and contain marginally more unique ideas. When a coding agent runs proof-of-concept experiments on the ideas, our model's success@k is comparable to Claude Opus 4.8's, so we see that the added diversity does not cost any executability.

candidates.title: Tree-Aware Posterior Distillation for Long-Horizon Agentic Reinforcement Learning
candidates.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has become a scalable post-training paradigm for large language models. However, training agents over long-horizon interactions presents two challenges: using only terminal rewards makes turn-level credit assignment sparse and high-variance, while sequential mini-batch updates on a fixed rollout batch introduce policy staleness as the current policy drifts from the behavior policy. Existing approaches obtain denser credit via learned critics, process reward models, or on-policy distillation, but they rely on a value network, step-level annotations, or a stronger external teacher that increase training complexity. Meanwhile, importance sampling and clipping mitigate policy drift, but they do not specify a finite target that stops sequential updates from overshooting. In this work, we introduce TreeOPSD, a critic-free, tree-aware posterior self-distillation framework for long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning. Treating each interaction turn as a tree node, TreeOPSD branches alternative continuations from shared prefixes and recursively backs up terminal rewards into implicit turn-level credit. It then maps each credit to a closed-form, bounded teacher distribution parameterized by the likelihood ratio relative to the frozen behavior policy. Minimizing the divergence between this teacher and the student policy recovers the policy-gradient direction as the tangent at the behavior policy while bounding updates toward a finite target across sequential mini-batches. Empirically, TreeOPSD improves agentic capabilities across several competitive benchmarks and model scales, especially for long-horizon tasks, e.g., raising the average accuracy of Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 by 4.97 points over GRPO on the Deep Research setting.

candidates.title: Where Does the Performance Go? Understanding and Recovering Performance Regressions in C-to-Rust Translation
candidates.abstract: Rust is increasingly adopted as a memory-safe successor to C, and transpilers such as \crust{} can migrate entire C projects while preserving their behavior. Preserving behavior, however, does not guarantee preserving performance. We study this gap on 20 real-world C projects and their \crust{} translations. On the eight projects used for analysis, the translated Rust is more than 3\% slower than the original C on 12 of 19 operations, by up to 62.2\%. By comparing execution-cost profiles, optimized LLVM IR, and compiler optimization remarks across each C--Rust pair, we trace these slowdowns to nine recurring performance issues, spanning residual runtime work, missed compiler optimizations, and C-style source patterns, and derive an optimization direction for each. We then present \ourtool{}, an LLM-based approach that encodes these issues as reusable optimization rules to recover the performance of translated Rust. \ourtool{} profiles each project to locate hot functions and matches them against rule-specific patterns. The LLM then checks each rule's rewrite preconditions against the project context before rewriting, and a rewrite is kept only if it passes both functional and performance validation. On 41 operations from twelve held-out projects, \ourtool{} preserves C outputs on all tested workloads and speeds up 40 operations over the \crust{} translations, 18 of which end up faster than the original C. It outperforms the general-purpose coding agent \codex{} on 31 of the 37 operations where both preserve C outputs, and outperforms its own variant without rule guidance on 34 of the 41 operations.

candidates.title:
"Ensemble Knowledge Distillation for Federated Semi-
Supervised Medical Image Classification"
A Mobile-Centric Approach to Improving the Performance of Decentralized Wireless Networks
candidates.abstract: The proliferation of wireless devices and intelligent environments has led to increasingly dense, interference-prone Wireless Local Area Network (WLAN) deployments. Recent amendments, such as IEEE 802.11ax/be, aim to enhance spatial reuse (SR) by optimizing spectrum efficiency. However, current SR initiatives face significant deployment challenges, including incompatibility with legacy 802.11 versions, a lack of centralized coordination, the difficulty for Access Points (APs) to monitor their neighborhood while maintaining uninterrupted service, and limited monitoring range. We argue that these limitations stem from the traditional AP-centric approach. In contrast, this work proposes a mobile-centric SR approach that overcomes these issues. Our method uses roaming mobile terminals (MTs) to independently monitor neighboring AP parameters (channel, transmission power, carrier-sense threshold), regardless of the 802.11 version or owner. After collecting local topological information, MTs execute a two-stage optimization: first, a local channel selection heuristic, followed by an algorithm that uses a pre-trained neural network to quickly evaluate and select the best transmission power and carrier-sense threshold for each in-range AP. MTs then broadcast these recommended parameters opportunistically using unassociated management frames, allowing them to be modified on the fly. By using a pre-trained model, our system does not need to learn in real time; consequently, network convergence is primarily governed by how quickly the mobile terminals explore and cover the deployment area, which depends on factors such as terminal speed, number of mobile terminals, trajectory characteristics, and pause times. Simulation results demonstrate that this mobile-centric approach quickly identifies near-optimal AP configurations, achieving throughput performance comparable to the reinforcement learning approaches considered in this study while exhibiting substantially shorter estimate

candidates.title:
A Queueing Theoretic Perspective on Low-Latency LLM Inference with
  Variable Token Length
candidates.abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) propel the prosperity of interactive AI
applications showcased by ChatGPT that demand timely response of inference
services. However, LLM inference is computation intensive and memory intensive,
and improper parameter configuration at LLM platforms may exacerbate the
inference time. In this paper, we analyze the impact of LLM output token
distribution on the inference queueing delay, where the max-token clipping and
the batched inference are considered. By formulating an M/G/1 model, we observe
that enforcing a maximum output token limit on a very small fraction of
inference requests can significantly reduce the queueing delay, and our model
facilitates the selection of the optimal limit. For the batch inference, we
model the service process as a bulk queue in which the batch processing time is
affected by the batch size and the maximum token size inside this batch
jointly. The queueing delays of the batching of all buffered requests (dynamic
batching), the batching of constant number of requests (fixed batching), and
the batching without intra-batch waiting (elastic batching) are derived.
Experimental results show that our mathematical models coincide with the
event-driven simulations well.
candidates.estimate_basis: 20 minute maximum bounded check allocation; not measured runtime

candidates.title: A Self-Improving Coding Agent
candidates.abstract:
Recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) have spurred interest in
deploying LLM agents to undertake tasks in the world. LLMs are often deployed
in agent systems: code that orchestrates LLM calls and provides them with
tools. We demonstrate that an agent system, equipped with basic coding tools,
can autonomously edit itself, and thereby improve its performance on benchmark
tasks. We find performance gains from 17% to 53% on a random subset of SWE
Bench Verified, with additional performance gains on LiveCodeBench, as well as
synthetically generated agent benchmarks. Our work represents an advancement in
the automated and open-ended design of agentic systems, and demonstrates a
data-efficient, non gradient-based learning mechanism driven by LLM reflection
and code updates.
candidates.estimate_basis: 20 minute maximum bounded check allocation; not measured runtime

candidates.title: A Study on the Intersection of GPU Utilization and CNN Inference
candidates.abstract:
There has been significant progress in developing neural network
architectures that both achieve high predictive performance and that also
achieve high application-level inference throughput (e.g., frames per second).
Another metric of increasing importance is GPU utilization during inference:
the measurement of how well a deployed neural network uses the computational
capabilities of the GPU on which it runs. Achieving high GPU utilization is
critical to increasing application-level throughput and ensuring a good return
on investment for deploying GPUs.
  This paper analyzes the GPU utilization of convolutional neural network (CNN)
inference. We first survey the GPU utilization of CNNs to show that there is
room to improve the GPU utilization of many of these CNNs. We then investigate
the GPU utilization of networks within a neural architecture search (NAS)
search space, and explore how using GPU utilization as a metric could
potentially be used to accelerate NAS itself. Our study makes the case that
there is room to improve the inference-time GPU utilization of CNNs and that
knowledge of GPU utilization has the potential to benefit even applications
that do not target utilization itself. We hope that the results of this study
will spur future innovation in designing GPU-efficient neural networks.
candidates.estimate_basis: 20 minute maximum bounded check allocation; not measured runtime

candidates.title: Accelerating Mixture-of-Experts Inference by Hiding Offloading Latency with Speculative Decoding
candidates.abstract: Recent advancements in Mixture of Experts (MoE) models have significantly increased their parameter scale as well as model performance. Extensive offloading techniques have been proposed to address the GPU memory limitations of MoE inference. However, due to the I/O bottleneck and sparse computation of MoE models, existing offloading techniques still suffer from low hardware utilization. To fully utilize the hardware resources, we propose SpecMoEOff, which employs the speculative decoding technique to enlarge the workload of each expert. SpecMoEOff orchestrates the GPU and CPU by both theoretical and empirical roofline analysis. In addition, we develop a dedicated CPU chunked attention verification kernel to fit the speculative decoding in offloading scenarios as well as minimizing the additional overhead led by draft models. SpecMoEOff further integrates an optimizer to automatically tune the hyperparameters of speculative decoding under given hardware and workload. Experimental results show that SpecMoEOff achieves up to 2.5x decode throughput improvement over the state-of-the-art MoE offloading techniques.
candidates.estimate_basis: 20 minute maximum bounded check allocation; not measured runtime

candidates.title:
AdaptInfer: Adaptive Token Pruning for Vision-Language Model Inference
  with Dynamical Text Guidance
candidates.abstract:
Vision-language models (VLMs) have achieved impressive performance on
multimodal reasoning tasks such as visual question answering (VQA), but their
inference cost remains a significant challenge due to the large number of
vision tokens processed during the prefill stage. Existing pruning methods
often rely on directly using the attention patterns or static text prompt
guidance, failing to exploit the dynamic internal signals generated during
inference. To address these issues, we propose AdaptInfer, a plug-and-play
framework for adaptive vision token pruning in VLMs. First, we introduce a
fine-grained, dynamic text-guided pruning mechanism that reuses layer-wise
text-to-text attention maps to construct soft priors over text-token
importance, allowing more informed scoring of vision tokens at each stage.
Second, we perform an offline analysis of cross-modal attention shifts and
identify consistent inflection locations in inference, which inspire us to
propose a more principled and efficient pruning schedule. Our method is
lightweight and plug-and-play, also generalizable across multi-modal tasks.
Experimental results have verified the effectiveness of the proposed method.
For example, it reduces CUDA latency by 61.3\% while maintaining an average
accuracy of 92.9\% on vanilla LLaVA-1.5-7B. Under the same token budget,
AdaptInfer surpasses SOTA in accuracy.

candidates.title: AgenTag: Attribution of AI Coding Agents from Behavioral Fingerprints
candidates.abstract: AI coding agents increasingly author pull requests (PRs), often under developers' own accounts, obscuring who actually produced a change. Reliable attribution is important for repository governance, empirical studies of AI-assisted software development, and measuring the impact of AI coding agents. Existing work focuses on closed-set identification of known agents, leaving the practical limits of open-world AI coding agent attribution largely unexplored. In this paper, we present AgenTag, a multimodal framework for open-world AI coding agent attribution, evaluated on AIDev, comprising 33,580 PRs from five AI coding agents and 6,618 human-authored PRs. We represent each PR using textual, behavioral, and code-based modalities, and compare conventional classification with supervised contrastive learning for open-set recognition and few-shot enrollment of previously unseen agents. AgenTag identifies authoring agents with a weighted F1 of 0.96 (macro F1 of 0.84), distinguishes AI- from human-authored PRs with a balanced F1 of 0.89, and detects previously unseen agents with an AUC of 0.84. We further show that PR descriptions and commit messages provide nearly all of the attribution signal, whereas code diffs contribute little across multiple representations, indicating that coding agents are distinguished primarily by how they communicate changes rather than by the code they generate. Moreover, these behavioral fingerprints persist after removing explicit self-disclosed markers, demonstrating that attribution relies largely on latent stylistic characteristics. These findings show that reliable attribution of AI coding agents is feasible and clarify the practical trade-offs between attribution accuracy and the information required to achieve it.
candidates.estimate_basis: 20 minute maximum bounded check allocation; not measured runtime

candidates.title: AgentCgroup: Understanding and Controlling OS Resources of AI Agents
candidates.abstract: AI agents are increasingly deployed in multi-tenant cloud environments, where they execute diverse tool calls within sandboxed containers, each call with distinct resource demands and rapid fluctuations. We present a systematic characterization of OS-level resource dynamics in sandboxed AI coding agents, analyzing 144 software engineering tasks from the SWE-rebench benchmark across two LLM models. Our measurements reveal that (1) OS-level execution (tool calls, container and agent initialization) accounts for 56-74% of end-to-end task latency; (2) memory, not CPU, is the concurrency bottleneck; (3) memory spikes are tool-call-driven with a up to 15.4x peak-to-average ratio; and (4) resource demands are highly unpredictable across tasks, runs, and models. Comparing these characteristics against serverless, microservice, and batch workloads, we identify three mismatches in existing resource controls: a granularity mismatch (container-level policies vs. tool-call-level dynamics), a responsiveness mismatch (user-space reaction vs. sub-second unpredictable bursts), and an adaptability mismatch (history-based prediction vs. non-deterministic stateful execution). We propose AgentCgroup, an intent-driven eBPF-based resource controller that exploits agents ability to declare resource needs and reconstruct execution strategies, using hierarchical cgroup structures aligned with tool-call boundaries, in-kernel enforcement via sched_ext and memcg_bpf_ops, and runtime-adaptive policies. Preliminary evaluation demonstrates improved multi-tenant isolation and reduced resource waste. AgentCgroup is open-source at https://github.com/eunomia-bpf/agentcgroup
candidates.estimate_basis: 20 minute maximum bounded check allocation; not measured runtime

candidates.title: Agentic Harness Engineering: Observability-Driven Automatic Evolution of Coding-Agent Harnesses
candidates.abstract: Harnesses are now central to coding-agent performance, mediating how models interact with tools and execution environments. Yet harness engineering remains a manual craft, because automating it faces a heterogeneous action space across editable components, voluminous trajectories that bury actionable signal, and edits whose effect is hard to attribute. We introduce Agentic Harness Engineering (AHE), a closed loop that addresses these challenges through three matched observability pillars: (1) component observability gives every editable harness component a file-level representation so the action space is explicit and revertible; (2) experience observability distills millions of raw trajectory tokens into a layered, drill-down evidence corpus that an evolving agent can actually consume; and (3) decision observability pairs every edit with a self-declared prediction, later verified against the next round's task-level outcomes. Together, these pillars turn every edit into a falsifiable contract, so harness evolution proceeds autonomously without collapsing into trial-and-error. Empirically, ten AHE iterations lift pass@1 on Terminal-Bench 2 from 69.7% to 77.0%, surpassing the human-designed harness Codex-CLI (71.9%) and the self-evolving baselines ACE and TF-GRPO. The frozen harness transfers without re-evolution: on SWE-bench-verified it tops aggregate success at 12% fewer tokens than the seed, and on Terminal-Bench 2 it yields +5.1 to +10.1pp cross-family gains across three alternate model families, indicating the evolved components encode general engineering experience rather than benchmark-specific tuning. Ablations localize the gain to tools, middleware, and long-term memory rather than the system prompt, suggesting factual harness structure transfers while prose-level strategy does not.
