candidates.title: Axiomatic World Modeling for Physics Reasoning
candidates.abstract: Recent research-level physics-reasoning benchmarks for LLMs reveal a failure mode that lies not in knowledge or execution, but in modeling the world being reasoned about. Models often silently alter given quantities, fabricate laws, or inject unstated assumptions to force a problem into familiar patterns, and then reason inside this corrupted world. We define this premise-level divergence as modeling drift: the gap between a model's internal axiomatic world model (AWM) and the true physical world specified in the problem. Although RLVR and PRM have yielded substantial gains in mathematics and code, their reward shapes do not directly supervise world modeling in axiomatic domains such as physics. We propose Reinforcement Learning with Axiomatic World Modeling (RLAWM), which optimizes the policy by penalizing divergence between its inferred axiomatic world model and the true physics world. RLAWM probes physics reasoning at two hierarchical levels (modeling and solving), each scored by a physically grounded reward. The modeling reward targets abstract knowledge formulation, evaluating whether the model captures the true axiomatic world before attempting calculation. The solving reward targets instantiated knowledge reasoning, checking whether the model's concrete derivation remains consistent with the axiomatic world. This two-level structure separates what world the model believes it is reasoning in from how it reasons within that world. The framework operates exclusively during training, with no extra cost during inference. RLAWM improves performance by up to +12.2 points on PhysReason and +5.2 on PHYSICS over the baseline. It also generalizes zero-shot across difficulty, source, and domain, with a 2.45x gain and +10 points over the strongest baseline on olympiad-level physics and math.

candidates.title: World Models with Configurable Perception
candidates.abstract: Real-world observations are noisy and often contain excessive task-irrelevant information. Effective world modeling and planning need to abstract observations into world state representations while filtering out irrelevant information. However, encoders in existing world models are typically non-adaptive, leading to state representations that are easily distracted by task-irrelevant information. As a result, the model may not selectively filter observations to cater to different task demands. To address this problem, we introduce ConfigWM, which realizes configurable perception through task-conditioned state extraction. Given a language description of the task at hand, ConfigWM uses it as a configuration signal to steer how visual embeddings are mapped into a task-specific state space, selectively preserving information relevant to the current task while suppressing task-irrelevant variations. Action-conditioned dynamics are then learned in this task-specific state space for planning. We evaluate ConfigWM in environments with increasing levels of distraction. While existing methods exhibit substantial declines in planning success rate as the environments become increasingly noisy, ConfigWM remains comparatively stable and outperforms the strongest competing method by 22.3% on average across diverse environments. Consistent gains in physical-quantity probing (+0.365 Pearson r) and distracted-to-clean retrieval (+75.5%) further indicate that ConfigWM learns states that preserve task-relevant information while remaining robust to distractors, supporting reliable world modeling and planning in noisy worlds. candidates.title: On the Tip of the Tongue: First-Token Cueing as a Behavioral Probe of Recall Failures in LLMs
candidates.abstract: Large language models often answer factual questions incorrectly in closed-book settings, and such errors are usually attributed to missing knowledge. Yet models often encode answers they fail to produce. We show that many closed-book errors are first-token recall failures: the model commits to a wrong first token, but once given the right one it completes the answer and often recognizes it as correct. We study this with First-Token Cueing, a behavioral probe that prefills the response with the first token of the gold answer. Model uncertainty peaks at the first answer token, where it already predicts correctness, and among gold prefixes of any length the first token alone accounts for the largest share of recovered errors. Across 16 open models, this one token corrects between a fifth and a half of the errors on multi-token answers in English QA and improves accuracy in all seven languages of a multilingual benchmark. Most of the errors it corrects are also solved by the model's own sampled reasoning, a criterion for encoded knowledge, and models recognize correct starts they do not produce: they continue a correct start more confidently than an incorrect start of the same answer type and prior probability, yet rarely find it without the gold answer. These results locate a recoverable class of factual errors at the first decoding step, where inference-time methods may gain the most.

candidates.title: Self-Credit: Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Agentic RL via Intra-group Rescaling
candidates.abstract: LLM agents are commonly trained with RLVR, but the sparse nature of typical RLVR rewards makes credit assignment challenging, especially for long-horizon tasks. We propose Self-Credit, an end-to-end agentic RL method that creates dense supervision signals from sparse outcome rewards using self-generated credit assignment via intra-group rescaling. Self-Credit builds on group-based RL with three components. First, during its rollouts, the policy model generates summaries with citations to earlier turns containing critical evidence, which serve as self-generated credit. Second, we refine this model-generated credit with intra-group rescaling, which compares cited actions across successful and failed rollouts for the same prompt. This approach uses group-level agreement and disagreement to remove undeserved credit and further emphasize credit assigned to critical actions. Third, advantage reweighting uses the rescaled credit weights to update the advantages of the cited turns. On BrowseComp-Plus, Self-Credit improves over the base models by 37.0 and 36.2 points on Qwen3 8B and 32B respectively, and outperforms the strongest agentic RL baselines by 8.5 and 5.6 points, respectively. Self-Credit also improves over the strongest baselines by 4.9 points on GAIA and 4.7 points on xBench-DeepSearch. Analyses show that self-generated credit provides useful signals for selecting critical actions, and that intra-group rescaling, especially on failed rollouts, is important across model scales.

candidates.title: EAU: Environment-Agent-User Co-evolution for Training User-Centric Agents
candidates.abstract: Training LLM agents to interact with users over multiple turns is challenging because the learning signal depends not only on the agent, but also on the user simulator and environment, which jointly shape the agent's experience. Simulated users can be stochastic or inconsistent, while environments may contain unreliable tools, incomplete state coverage, and incorrect verifiers. Prior work mainly addresses the resulting instability through reward shaping or denser supervision, while treating these components as fixed. We instead introduce EAU, a meta-agent framework for environment--agent--user co-evolution. During training, EAU monitors trajectories, tool traces, rewards, and training statistics; diagnoses failures and uninformative interactions; and proposes targeted modifications to the user simulator, environment, reward design, and RL configuration. Validated changes are hot-swapped into the ongoing run, allowing the training setup to evolve together with the policy. These adaptations also persist across runs, so later training can build on previously discovered improvements rather than restarting from a fixed setup. We enable this process through an editable symbolic representation of user and environment dynamics, while the agent remains a neural LLM optimized with RL. Across three interactive-agent benchmarks and two backbone models, EAU consistently outperforms prior RL methods, improving the overall score over the strongest baseline by 14.7--15.0% and increasing successful task completion on ColBench by up to 36.7%, showing that co-evolving the training system with the policy can substantially improve multi-turn RL.

candidates.title: HallucinationNerd: A Framework and Tool to Detect Hallucinations and Unsupported Claims
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), agentic systems, and human authors produce text with inline citations, but the cited sources do not always support the claims attributed to them. We present HallucinationNerd, a modular citation-verification engine that decomposes text into atomic claims, retrieves relevant passages from each cited source, and determines whether the source supports the claim. In addition, HallucinationNerd identifies claims that carry no citation and searches user-approved databases to find or refute supporting evidence for them. The system handles five common citation formats, operates on PDFs, web pages, and plain text, and produces per-claim verdicts with evidence pointers. The underlying algorithm mixes parsing (to identify claim&ndash;citation pairs), overlapped chunking, stopword elimination, and AI-based semantic comparison. In head-to-head comparison on the same data, HallucinationNerd substantially outperforms (by about 20% in F1 score) state-of-the-art systems on accuracy and precision on a benchmark built from research papers. HallucinationNerd can also be used to verify the output of other AI systems. For example, we audited a set of outputs of Scholar GPT, a publicly available scholarly research agent. In that sample at least, its citations were faithful to the cited sources.

candidates.title: Cryptanalysis and Improved Image Cryptosystem via Chaos and Convolutional Neural Network
candidates.abstract: Chaos-based image encryption schemes are often motivated by the apparent randomness of chaotic sequences and by the nonlinear processing capability of convolutional neural networks (CNNs). However, these properties alone do not guarantee cryptographic security. In this work, we present a systematic cryptanalysis of an image-encryption framework combining Logistic-map dynamics, pixel permutation, XOR masking, CNN-based processing, image hiding, and wavelet-domain operations. Under the fixed-state condition considered in our analysis, the reversible encryption core can be reduced to c=&Pi;(p)&oplus;s, where &Pi; is a plaintext-independent permutation and s is a fixed byte-wise mask. The effective secret is therefore characterized by the equivalent pair (&Pi;,s), rather than by the nominal parameters of the underlying chaotic map. Based on this structural reduction, we derive mask-cancellation and differential relations and develop five complementary cryptanalytic methods: chosen-plaintext, known-plaintext, chosen-ciphertext, differential, and model-class black-box attacks. The chosen-plaintext attack recovers the XOR mask from an all-zero query and determines the permutation using position-labelled inputs. The known-plaintext attack constructs cross-sample XOR fingerprints to progressively identify permutation positions when the available plaintexts provide sufficient diversity. The chosen-ciphertext and differential attacks recover the inverse mapping or eliminate the fixed mask through carefully designed query pairs. The black-box attack further uses multi-byte coordinate encoding to identify the complete fixed input&ndash;output transformation without prior knowledge of the block structure. These attacks do not require recovery of the Logistic-map parameters; instead, they directly reconstruct the equivalent transformation required to decrypt ciphertexts generated under the same induced state. In addition, for the explicitly linear fixed-convolution component of the target framework, we perform a separate conditional impulse-response experiment to recover its effective convolution kernel. Experiments on 128&times;128 grayscale images with 16&times;16 blocks demonstrate exact byte-level plaintext recovery for the analyzed fixed-state reversible core, while also showing that known-plaintext recovery depends on sample diversity. The results indicate that reusable and separable permutation&ndash;mask structures remain vulnerable even when embedded in chaos- and CNN-assisted image-processing pipelines, motivating per-image state diversification and stronger key-dependent coupling between permutation and diffusion.

candidates.title: Relational Narrative Historiography: A Higher-Order Framework for Representing Competing Historical Narratives
candidates.abstract: This paper presents Relational Narrative Historiography (RNH) as a framework paper and testable research hypothesis, not as an empirical study. Historical accounts of the same event frequently diverge across archives, languages, and interpretive communities&mdash;a challenge that extends to any domain where reports conflict or facts remain disputed. Conventional knowledge graphs and Large Language Models may favour frequently represented or dominant accounts, potentially reducing the visibility of minority perspectives and of the uncertainty inherent in contested information. This paper proposes that narratives&mdash;or more generally, contested information bundles&mdash;can be represented as higher-order objects that bind events, claims, actors, sources, locations, temporal anchors, interpretive frames, and internal relations. We introduce Relational Narrative Historiography (RNH), a hypergraph-based framework in which narratives are first-class objects. Unlike pairwise graph models, which represent a narrative through separate narrative nodes and edges, hypergraphs can keep the membership of a narrative explicit and represent higher-order relationships as a single structure. The framework uses three epistemic constructs: Epistemic Weight (the strength of evidence supporting a narrative), Divergence (the quantitative distance between narratives), and Uncertainty (what remains unresolved). We describe the conceptual architecture and mathematical formulation, illustrate the calculations with a numerical example based on semantic similarity, and outline an evaluation protocol. All numerical values presented in the worked example are illustrative and are not derived from any expert-annotated real-world dataset. RNH is proposed as a framework and testable research hypothesis, but its validity still needs to be examined empirically in digital humanities, AI, and knowledge representation.

candidates.title: Thermal-Aware Generative Adversarial Augmentation for Small-Sample Induction-Motor Fault Detection Using Infrared Thermography
candidates.abstract: Fault diagnosis in induction motors is challenging when only a limited number of labeled infrared thermal images are available for training. Effective small-sample augmentation requires generated images to preserve class-related appearance patterns as well as visual realism. To address this challenge, a thermal-aware generative adversarial network (TA-GAN) is proposed for induction-motor fault diagnosis using pseudo-colour infrared images. An adaptive attention module combines feature intensity and Sobel-gradient information to emphasize component&ndash;state-related thermal patterns. A dual-branch critic jointly evaluates global and attention-weighted features, while an appearance-consistency loss constrains bright-region intensity, gradient structure, and spatial position during generation. The trained generator augments the limited real samples, and the combined dataset is used to train a lightweight classifier. Experiments on acquisition-batch-separated data partitions show improved classification performance over the evaluated real-only baselines under matched classifier-training budgets. The complete framework performs best among the evaluated component and individual-loss configurations. Generated-sample evaluation further indicates improved appearance similarity to real training images compared with a basic conditional GAN, while evaluation on a different motor provides additional evidence of transfer under the tested conditions. Image generation is performed offline, allowing the deployed system to retain the lightweight MobileNetV4 classifier architecture.

candidates.title: More Data, Worse Inference: How the Imputation Model Decides an Interaction Effect
candidates.abstract: Interaction hypotheses are central to psychology, and predictors are often incomplete.Standard guidance recommends multiple imputation (MI), yet "MI" denotes differentprocedures once the model contains a product term. We quantify how the imputation modelgoverns recovery of a continuous × continuous interaction when one predictor is missing.The simulation spans N = 20–160, 20% and 40% missingness, and both missing-at-random(MAR) and missing-completely-at-random (MCAR), with 1000 replications per cell and MonteCarlo standard errors. We compare six methods: listwise deletion, mean imputation,deterministic regression imputation, and three MI variants — naive,Just-Another-Variable (JAV), and substantive-model-compatible (SMC-FCS). CongenialSMC-FCS recovered the interaction with near-nominal coverage; JAV's bias crossed zerounder MAR, reaching +0.017 at N = 160 (4.1 Monte Carlo standard errors), as Seaman etal. (2012) predict. Under MAR, naive MI — whose imputation model omits the interaction —attenuated the coefficient by approximately the missing fraction (bias ≈ −π·β₃; aboutthree-quarters of π under MCAR). Because this bias persists while the standard errorshrinks, 95% coverage collapsed to 0.758 at the largest sample size — worsening, notimproving, as data accrued. Deterministic regression imputation manufactured a spuriousinteraction, inflating Type I error to 0.276 under MAR against a nominal 0.05; it isabsent under MCAR and governed by one verified selection moment, the shift outcome- orcovariate-dependent missingness induces in the observed moderator. For interactions,"multiple imputation" and "full-information maximum likelihood" (Lüdtke et al., 2020)name families, and the member matters more than the label.

candidates.title: Vision-language models and visual foundation models in neurosurgery
candidates.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Visual foundation models (VFMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) offer adaptable approaches to neurosurgical imaging, segmentation, intraoperative assistance, and clinical decision support. However, the available evidence varies substantially in model type, supervision, validation setting, and clinical task, and their readiness for routine clinical use remains uncertain.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted a narrative review of peer-reviewed primary research reports published between January 2020 and August 2026, identified through PubMed, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar. Studies evaluating visual, vision-language, or multimodal foundation models in neurosurgical applications were included. Supervised Vision Transformer (ViT) and ViT–CNN systems were retained as contemporary transformer-based comparator studies but were not classified as foundation models. Evidence was synthesised according to model adaptation, clinical application, within-study comparative performance, validation setting, and translational limitations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Seven studies met the review criteria. FastGlioma provided a prospective multicentre evaluation of a visual foundation model for intraoperative detection of glioma infiltration. In lumbar-spine MRI, zero-shot SAM and MedSAM performed below supervised nnU-Net on segmentation metrics. A task-adapted SAM2-UNet system achieved a mean Dice score of 0.771 for brain-tumour segmentation, although its mean IoU was 0.569 compared with 0.571 for Mask R-CNN in the reported comparison. Supervised transformer-based systems demonstrated performance in acute traumatic brain injury triage and vertebral fracture classification, although the latter combined ViT, CNN, ensemble fusion, and GAN-based augmentation. In multimodal reasoning, GPT-4o achieved higher absolute diagnostic accuracy than CNS-Obsidian, whereas CNS-Obsidian had higher length-adjusted diagnostic accuracy. Evidence for clinical translation remained limited by heterogeneous validation settings, incomplete reporting of computational performance and safety outcomes, predominantly single-centre or preclinical evaluations, and limited assessment of patient outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Foundation-model-based systems show potential across selected neurosurgical tasks, but current evidence is insufficient to establish routine clinical readiness or patient benefit. Reported results are primarily task-specific and should not be interpreted as evidence of a general architectural advantage. Future studies should evaluate these systems prospectively under human supervision while determining whether clinicians can reliably detect and mitigate erroneous outputs. Multi-centre validation, uncertainty assessment, computational efficiency, workflow integration, and patient-centred outcomes should be prioritised.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

candidates.title: NeoWorld-3: From Pixels to Code-Defined Physical Worlds
candidates.abstract: Simulation-ready world reconstruction demands physical interactivity beyond visual realism, which existing black-box 3D generation fails to deliver. We present NeoWorld-3, a coding-agent framework that reconstructs interactive 3D worlds from visual observations via tunable, executable programs. At its core, NeoSDK provides the underlying computational engine for low-level geometries, part composition, differentiable parameter refinement, and physics validation. At the same time, NeoMCP exposes these capabilities as structured, tool-callable APIs for vision-language agents to visually inspect, edit code, and iteratively refine programs. Through a hierarchical coordinator-worker architecture, the framework scales seamlessly from standalone articulated objects to complex compositional scenes. Evaluations across object-level and scene-level reconstruction benchmarks demonstrate that NeoWorld-3 achieves state-of-the-art geometric fidelity and physical readiness. Crucially, manipulation trajectories planned within our reconstructed twins achieve successful zero-shot execution on a physical dual-arm robot, completing the Real-Sim-Real loop.
